name: The Catalytic Mile
description:
The Catalytic Mile is Detroit's cultural preservation district — a roughly one-mile stretch of Woodward Avenue anchored by the Detroit Institute of Arts on one end and the Wayne State University Cognitive Sciences Campus on the other. The name is corporate marketing, coined by the Palladian Construction subsidiary that rebuilt the district in the 2060s, referencing both the catalytic converter (automotive heritage) and the idea of cultural catalysis. Locals just call it Midtown, because they called it that before the corps arrived and they'll call it that after the corps leave, assuming the corps ever leave.

The DIA survived the collapse years because someone — the historical record is deliberately vague about who — negotiated a cultural preservation easement with Cinderblock AI in exchange for data rights to every visitor's neural interface. The museum still stands, its Diego Rivera murals intact behind climate-controlled glass, and every person who looks at them has their aesthetic response recorded, analyzed, and sold on the Tessera Behavioral Exchange. Rivera would have appreciated the irony. Wayne State University was absorbed into the Tessera Academic Partnership Network in 2158, its cognitive sciences department becoming one of Tessera's primary research feeders. The campus is technically independent. The funding is not.

The district between these two anchors is a curated bohemia — galleries, performance spaces, restaurants, and residential blocks designed to feel organic while being entirely corporate-planned. Artists live here on subsidized leases, producing work that makes the district attractive to the Tier 3 residents whose rents actually pay for things. It's a terrarium. The art is real, the community is real, the subsidies create a dependency structure that means the entire cultural ecosystem exists at the pleasure of the corporate landlords. Pull the subsidies and the Mile dies in six months. Everyone knows this. Nobody says it at gallery openings.

sights: The DIA's Beaux-Arts facade preserved in amber — literally encased in transparent protective shielding
Street murals refreshed by AR overlay, the original paint preserved beneath digital augmentation layers
Wayne State's cognitive sciences tower, its upper floors glowing with Tessera branding after dark
Gallery windows displaying art that your neural interface automatically prices and attributes
Students and artists mixing on Woodward, distinguishable by the age of their augments
sounds: Live music from subsidized venues — jazz, electronic, neo-Motown, all of it genuine, all of it funded
The murmur of gallery crowds, punctuated by the soft chime of neural interface art-purchase confirmations
University lecture broadcasts leaking from open windows — cognitive science terminology in excited voices
Street performers who are actually good, because the bad ones get algorithmically de-prioritized by the district management AI
The 5 PM autonomous transit chime, when the subsidized artist shuttles run to cheaper districts
smells: Coffee and paint thinner — the two fuels of the creative class
Restaurant row along Cass Avenue, where the food is excellent and the prices exclude anyone below Tier 2
Old building materials — the district preserved some original structures, and they smell like history slowly losing to chemistry
atmosphere.feel: Beautiful and compromised. The Catalytic Mile feels like a place where genuine creativity happens inside a corporate terrarium. The art is real. The music is real. The community is real. The fact that all of it exists because a construction corponation decided cultural districts increase adjacent property values by 23% does not make the art less real. It makes everything else less honest.

demographics: Approximately 45,000 residents. A mix of subsidized artists (Tier 1-2), university students and faculty (Tier 2-3), and the Tier 3-4 professionals whose market-rate rents cross-subsidize the entire district. The demographic balance is carefully managed by Palladian's district algorithms.
economy: Cultural tourism, university research funding, gallery sales, and the invisible economy of neural data harvested from every aesthetic experience in the district. The DIA alone generates Φ2.1 billion annually in behavioral data licensing.
power_structure: Palladian Construction owns the land and manages the district through an AI-driven property management system called the Curator. Wayne State's administration answers to the Tessera Academic Partnership Board. The artists' cooperative has a seat at district planning meetings but no vote.
dangers: Subsidy dependency — cross the wrong corporate sponsor and lose your housing in 30 days
Neural data harvesting — every aesthetic experience in the district is recorded and monetized
Academic surveillance — Wayne State research is monitored for commercially exploitable discoveries
Gentrification pressure — the district's success constantly pushes outward, consuming adjacent neighborhoods
The Curator algorithm — Palladian's district AI makes residency decisions that no human reviews
opportunities: Access to Wayne State's cognitive sciences research — cutting-edge BCI work with less security than a corporate lab
The artist community is a network of people who see things differently — valuable for intelligence and perspective
Gallery openings are where corporate executives drop their guard and talk to people they consider harmless
story_hooks: A Wayne State researcher discovers that the DIA's neural harvesting system has been modified to do more than record — it's been inserting cognitive suggestions into visitors for years
The Curator algorithm is about to terminate subsidies for an entire block of artist housing. The residents have 30 days to find Φ4 million or become homeless.
A student collective has been using Wayne State's cognitive lab after hours to develop open-source BCI firmware — Tessera has noticed
frequented_by: Artists and musicians on corporate subsidy
Tier 3 professionals who want to feel culturally engaged
Data brokers harvesting aesthetic response patterns
